nodes.title: AWS Lambda: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Lambda runs your code in response to events (API call, S3 upload, EventBridge schedule, SQS message). No servers to manage. You pay for invocations and execution time. The exam tests limits, cold starts, triggers, and the IAM execution role.

flashcards.front: Lambda execution limits — memory, time, payload?
flashcards.back: Memory: 128 MB - 10 GB (CPU scales with memory). Timeout: max 15 minutes. Sync invocation payload: 6 MB. Async invocation payload: 256 KB. Deployment package (zipped): 50 MB direct upload, 250 MB via S3, 10 GB via container image.

flashcards.front: Cold start — what is it and how do you minimize it?
flashcards.back: First invocation of an idle function takes 100 ms - 2 s extra to load the runtime and your code. Mitigations: provisioned concurrency (pre-warmed instances), smaller deployment packages, native-compiled runtimes (Go, Rust), keeping connections out of the handler so they're reused across invocations.

flashcards.front: Sync vs async vs poll-based invocation.
flashcards.back: Sync (API Gateway, ALB): caller waits for result. Async (S3, SNS, EventBridge): Lambda queues and retries on failure. Poll-based (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams): Lambda pulls records, processes in batches, manages retries via the source. Each has different retry semantics — read the docs.

flashcards.front: How does Lambda get permissions to call other AWS services?
flashcards.back: Each function has an IAM execution role. The role's policies say what the function CAN do (read S3, write DynamoDB, decrypt KMS). Lambda assumes the role on every invocation and exposes temporary credentials to your code via the SDK.

questions.q: A team must continuously deliver clickstream events to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet, with no code to manage shards or consumer applications, while batching events into roughly 5-minute files. Which AWS service is the best fit?
choices: Amazon Data Firehose with Parquet format conversion enabled and a 300-second buffer interval
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with a custom Lambda consumer that writes Parquet to S3 each minute
Amazon MSK Connect running a Kafka Connect S3 sink the team configures and tunes for Parquet
AWS Glue streaming ETL job triggered every five minutes from an Amazon EventBridge schedule
questions.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) is fully managed, can convert incoming records to Parquet or ORC, and natively buffers by size or by time interval (up to 900 seconds) before writing to S3 — no shards or consumer applications to operate. Kinesis Data Streams requires you to build and scale a consumer application yourself. MSK Connect on Kafka Connect adds Kafka topology and connector tuning the team explicitly wants to avoid. Glue streaming jobs run continuously rather than on a 5-minute schedule and would need additional configuration to land Parquet files cleanly.

questions.q: A Kinesis Data Streams application must keep events for the same user_id strictly in order, while scaling throughput across many users. How should producers configure each record?
choices: Set the explicit hash key to a random value so writes are distributed evenly across every shard
Use the user_id as the partition key so all records for one user hash to the same shard in order
Configure each producer to write to a single fixed shard to guarantee in-order delivery for users
Aggregate user events client-side and write one batched record per minute regardless of user id
questions.explanation: Kinesis preserves ordering within a single shard, and a record's partition key determines which shard it lands on. Using user_id as the partition key keeps per-user ordering while spreading aggregate load across many shards. Randomizing the explicit hash key would scatter the same user's events across shards and break ordering. Pinning all writes to a single shard caps throughput at one shard's limits (1 MB/s, 1000 records/s). Minute-level client-side batching introduces latency and loses per-event ordering granularity.

questions.q: A team must capture every row-level INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE from an Amazon RDS for MySQL database and continuously land the changes in an S3 data lake with minimal load on the source database. Which approach is the best fit?
choices: Schedule an hourly AWS Glue JDBC full-table extract and overwrite the S3 dataset on each run
Enable a DynamoDB stream on the table and forward records to S3 with an AWS Lambda consumer
Use AWS DMS in CDC mode reading the MySQL binary log with an S3 target endpoint
Run a nightly mysqldump on the RDS instance and upload the resulting SQL file to the S3 bucket
questions.explanation: AWS DMS CDC reads the MySQL binary log to capture row-level inserts, updates, and deletes with low impact on the source, and an S3 target endpoint writes the ongoing changes into the lake. An hourly Glue full extract re-scans the whole table each run, missing intra-hour deletes and putting heavy repeated load on the source. DynamoDB streams only exist on DynamoDB tables, not RDS for MySQL, so they cannot capture RDS changes. A nightly mysqldump is a full snapshot, not continuous CDC, and cannot represent individual delete operations between dumps.

questions.q: A near-real-time pipeline ingests events with Amazon Data Firehose and must enrich each record by adding a derived field before the data lands in S3, with the least operational overhead. Which approach should the team use?
choices: Land the raw records in S3 first, then run a separate scheduled Glue job to add the derived field afterward
Switch the destination to Amazon Redshift and compute the derived field with a post-load SQL UPDATE statement
Attach an AWS Lambda transformation function to the Firehose stream to enrich each record buffer in flight
Replace Firehose with Kinesis Data Streams and write a Kinesis Client Library consumer that performs the enrichment
questions.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose supports an inline AWS Lambda transformation that invokes on each buffered batch of records, letting you enrich or reshape data before it is delivered to S3 with no separate pipeline to operate. Landing raw data then running a scheduled Glue job adds a second stage and latency the requirement seeks to avoid. Routing to Redshift and post-processing with SQL changes the destination and adds a database the design does not need. Replacing Firehose with Kinesis Data Streams plus a custom KCL consumer reintroduces exactly the shard- and consumer-management overhead that Firehose was chosen to eliminate.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An AWS Glue Spark job reads daily files from an S3 prefix and must process only newly arrived files on each run, without re-scanning previously ingested data. Which Glue feature should be enabled on the job?
choices: Pushdown predicates configured per partition column in the source DynamicFrame transform
Glue triggers set to a fixed cron schedule so old partitions are not re-read by the workflow
Workflow run properties carrying the latest processed date that the job reads at startup
Glue job bookmarks, which persist a per-source watermark and skip data from previous runs
questions.explanation: Job bookmarks store state (file names, timestamps, or row counts depending on source type) across runs, so the next execution resumes from the last processed point and does not re-read older S3 files. Pushdown predicates filter known partitions at read time but do not automatically track progress between runs. Triggers only schedule a job — they have no memory of what was processed. Workflow run properties require the developer to track and pass state manually, which Glue bookmarks do natively.

questions.q: A daily Glue ETL job writes its output to S3 as thousands of small files, and downstream Athena queries are slow because of the large number of tiny objects. Which change most directly improves read performance for the downstream queries?
choices: Increase the Glue worker type to G.2X so each task has more memory while still emitting one file per partition key value
Coalesce or repartition the output DynamicFrame/DataFrame so the job writes fewer, larger files per partition
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket so the small files are read back to Athena faster
Switch the job to write CSV instead of Parquet so each row group is smaller and parses more quickly in Athena
questions.explanation: The small-files problem is solved by reducing file count: coalescing or repartitioning before the write produces fewer, larger objects (ideally 128 MB+), which cuts the per-object overhead Athena pays when listing and opening files. Increasing worker size gives more memory but does not change the number of output files. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads over the public internet and has no effect on Athena read latency for many small files. Switching to CSV makes things worse — CSV is row-oriented and loses columnar pruning, increasing bytes scanned.

questions.q: An Apache Spark job on Amazon EMR repeatedly fails with executor out-of-memory errors when joining a very large fact table to a small lookup table. Which optimization most directly addresses the failure?
choices: Increase the number of shuffle partitions so each task processes a larger slice of the join in one pass
Use a broadcast join to send the small lookup to every executor and skip shuffling the large table
Cache the large fact table in memory with persist(MEMORY_ONLY) before performing the join operation
Disable speculative execution so executors do not duplicate tasks and consume additional heap memory
questions.explanation: A broadcast join ships the small lookup table to every executor and joins locally, avoiding the expensive shuffle and skew that drive executor OOMs when one side of the join is large. Increasing shuffle partitions actually makes each task smaller, not larger — and the option's reasoning is inverted. Caching the large fact table in memory consumes more heap and worsens the OOM. Disabling speculative execution affects retried straggler tasks, not the memory pressure caused by shuffling a large join.

questions.q: Regulatory archives must remain on Amazon S3 for seven years, are accessed less than once per quarter, and may be retrieved within a 12-hour window when needed. Which storage class minimizes cost while still meeting that retrieval window?
choices: S3 Standard, which keeps archives immediately accessible at the highest per-GB storage cost
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which charges higher storage in exchange for millisecond access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest-cost class, with a standard retrieval time of about 12 hours
S3 One Zone-IA, which is cheaper than Standard-IA but stores data in only one availability zone
questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive has the lowest per-GB storage cost on S3; its standard retrieval time is up to 12 hours, which exactly fits the SLA. S3 Standard is the most expensive tier and unnecessary for quarterly access. Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more per GB in exchange for millisecond reads the workload does not need. One Zone-IA reduces durability/resilience but never reaches Glacier-tier pricing for long-term archives.

questions.q: A Redshift fact table with billions of rows is joined daily to a 50-million-row customer dimension on customer_id. Which distribution choice minimizes data shuffle during the join?
choices: DISTSTYLE KEY on customer_id for both tables so matching rows land on the same compute slice
DISTSTYLE EVEN on both tables so each slice carries an equal share of rows for parallel processing
DISTSTYLE ALL on the fact table so every node holds the full copy used during the join phase
DISTSTYLE AUTO on the fact table and DISTSTYLE ALL on the 50-million-row customer dimension
questions.explanation: When two tables share the same DISTKEY, Redshift co-locates rows with matching key values on the same slice and the join executes locally with no network shuffle. DISTSTYLE EVEN distributes rows round-robin, so matching customer_id rows scatter across slices and force a redistribution at join time. DISTSTYLE ALL on a billion-row fact would be impractically large (each node holds the full copy). DISTSTYLE ALL is intended for small lookup tables (typically a few million rows); a 50-million-row dimension wastes considerable storage on every node.

questions.q: A DynamoDB table keyed on date_only (YYYY-MM-DD) throttles heavily on writes each day because every new record hits the same partition. Which redesign best spreads write load while preserving efficient daily lookups?
choices: Add a random suffix to the date partition key and use Scan with FilterExpression to read by date
Switch the table to provisioned mode at a much higher write capacity to absorb the daily spike
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) so writes are cached and asynchronously batched to the base table
Use a high-cardinality field such as order_id as the partition key with date_only as the sort key
questions.explanation: Promoting a high-cardinality attribute (order_id) to the partition key spreads writes across many partitions and eliminates the hot partition; keeping date_only as the sort key still allows efficient per-day Query operations via a GSI on date_only or a partition-overloaded design. A random suffix would spread writes but force expensive Scan + FilterExpression to read by date. Raising provisioned capacity does not fix data skew — a single partition still caps at ~1000 WCU/3000 RCU. DAX is a read-through cache for reads and does not absorb write traffic.

questions.q: An Athena workload scans a JSON dataset partitioned by event_date and is both slow and expensive. The team wants the largest reduction in bytes scanned with minimal query rewrites. Which change has the greatest impact?
choices: Re-encode the JSON files using gzip compression so each query downloads fewer total bytes from S3
Convert the underlying data to Apache Parquet so Athena reads only the columns each query selects
Switch the Athena engine version to the latest release available in the workgroup configuration
Increase the per-query data scanned limit in the workgroup so larger result sets are not throttled
questions.explanation: Parquet is a columnar format, so Athena reads only the columns referenced by a query; combined with partition pruning this typically reduces bytes scanned (and Athena cost) by an order of magnitude or more. Gzipped JSON is still row-oriented — every query reads the full row even to project a single column. Engine version upgrades give marginal gains for the same data layout. Raising the workgroup scan limit caps cost runaway but does not lower per-query bytes scanned.

questions.q: A pipeline must run nightly with up to fifty interdependent Python tasks, retry logic per task, and rich DAG visualization familiar to the existing data team. Which orchestrator is the best fit?
choices: AWS Step Functions Standard workflow with one state per task and per-state retry policies on errors
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rules that fire each task at a specific time and order independently
Amazon MWAA, the managed Apache Airflow service that runs Python DAGs with task-level retries
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines orchestrating the data tasks as steps inside a single training pipeline
questions.explanation: Amazon MWAA (managed Airflow) is purpose-built for Python-centric DAGs with per-task retries and the familiar Airflow web UI for DAG visualization. Step Functions excels at orchestrating AWS service calls and supports per-state retries, but it lacks Airflow's Python-DAG ergonomics and visualization the team already knows. EventBridge Scheduler fires jobs at a time but offers no dependency graph between tasks. SageMaker Pipelines is an ML-pipeline primitive — not the right tool for a general 50-task Python ETL graph.
